newsitem.title: USA: U.S. suspends wheat export certificates to Turkey.
newsitem.headline: U.S. suspends wheat export certificates to Turkey.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Department has stopped issuing export certificates for wheat shipments to Turkey, and is considering halting export licenses for other commodities headed for Turkey, including corn and soybeans, a USDA official said Monday.
The USDA action was taken Oct 18, and was in response to the recent implemenation by Turkey of a zero-tolerance policy on wheat in regards to a large group of diseases.

The new Turkish policy has resulted so far in the rejection last week of one 15,000 tonne shipload of U.S. wheat, and could impact another 100,000 tonnes of American wheat enroute to Turkey, according to the U.S. agricultural counselor in Ankara.

The wheat was rejected after Turkish inspectors found traces of the grain fungus ergot in the shipload. Grain industry analaysts and USDA officials have said that it is virtually impossible to guarantee a complete absense of ergot, and that the allowable 0.05 pct amount is low and does not pose any health hazards.

"We have suspended issuing export certificates for all wheat to Turkey until this is resolved," said Jonathon Jones of USDA's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service. "Until Turkey changes its policy, no wheat will leave the United States for Turkey."

Jones said that APHIS is also considering halting export certificates for other commodities to Turkey if the issue is not settled. "Potentially this could impact a whole host of other grains to Turkey," he told Reuters.
Turkey bought around 520,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat in 1995/96, 600,000 tonnes of U.S. corn, a little over 100,000 tonnes of soybeans, and around 75,000 tonnes of soybean meal.
Turkey also purchased around 187,000 tonnes of U.S. rice in the 1995/96 marketing year, along with 43,800 bales of cotton.

While some analysts said Turkey was stopping wheat imports because of surplus domestic supplies this year, Turkish officials have told the U.S. government that the country is trying to enforce its regulations "in concert" with the way the European Union implements its agricultural import rules.
The U.S. agricultural counselor in Ankara met Turkey's minister of agriculture last week on the issue.

At that time, Washington obtained an agreement from Turkey that if the United States can prove Europe in fact does not have a zero-tolerance policy, Turkey will reassess its policy and hopefully back down from the zero-tolerance position.
U.S. officials said that European plant quarantine experts are now clarifying the EU position to Turkey, and that they are optimistic the issue will be resolved soon.

Ergot is a fungus that is widespread throughout the world. In large quantities it can be toxic to man and animals, but does not affect crop yields. Ergot occurs on a wide range of cereal products, including wheat, sorghum and barley.
